abstract: "Climate change is often understood as a psychologically distant threat. This paper asks whether extreme weather near a politician\u2019s geographic home changes how climate impacts are described in parliamentary speech. I combine sentence-level annotations of 28,448 European Parliament speeches with two exposure registers: a meteorological record of locally unusual warm spells and a disaster impact register of recorded floods, storms, and other climate-related events. Both are analysed at the MEP-speech-day level using three adjacent 30-day pre-speech windows, a 30-day future-exposure placebo, MEP and calendar-date fixed effects, and country-clustered inference. The primary meteorological estimate is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero (0.059 percentage points; p = 0.151); its 90% confidence interval excludes effects larger than 0.026 outcome standard deviations. The summer-heat specification is also null. In the disaster register, the primary occurrence-and-impact dose combines event frequency with the logged number of people affected and killed. Its immediate proximity estimate is positive but uncertain (0.060 percentage points; clustered p = 0.099; wild-cluster p = 0.112), with an equivalence bound of 0.024 outcome standard deviations. An unweighted event-count robustness is nominally significant (p = 0.030) but does not survive adjustment across temporal windows. The evidence rules out large changes in elite climate framing and provides limited evidence of a small immediate association following nearby recorded disasters."
